stem: A marketing coordinator types "Write a product launch email." into Claude and gets a generic, 600-word message that mentions none of the product's features. Which single change to the prompt would most improve the first draft?

options.text: Switch to the most capable model in the model picker, since a stronger model can work out what a launch email for this product should say.
options.why: No model can know the product, audience or facts that were never provided; the gap is in the prompt, not the model tier.

options.text: Add "Make it excellent, professional and engaging" to the end of the prompt.
options.why: Vague quality adjectives give Claude nothing concrete to act on; they do not tell it who the reader is or what to say.

options.text: State the audience, the goal of the email, the tone, a length limit and the three features that must be mentioned.
options.why: Audience, goal, format constraints and required facts are the context Claude needs; the help centre's advice is to write as if briefing someone with no background on the task.

options.text: Send the same prompt again in a new chat so Claude starts fresh.
options.why: A fresh chat with the same underspecified prompt produces another generic draft; nothing about the request has changed.

explanation: Claude responds to what it is told. An effective prompt states who the output is for, what it must achieve, the format and length, the constraints, and the facts it must include. Adjectives like "excellent", a stronger model or a retry do not supply the missing context.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer; Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

stem: An HR business partner pastes a job description for a customer-success manager into Claude and asks "Give me interview questions." She gets 30 questions of mixed quality, including several about technical skills the role does not need. She wants a structured set she can hand to a panel of four interviewers. Which rewritten prompt best fits?

options.text: "Give me better interview questions than last time, and leave out the technical ones."
options.why: "Better" is not a specification. Claude still does not know how many questions, which competencies matter, or what format the panel needs.

options.text: "Act as an experienced HR interviewer. Using the job description below, write 8 behavioural questions, each mapped to one of the five competencies it lists. Return a table with columns: competency, question, what a strong answer includes."
options.why: This gives a role, the source to work from, the number and type of questions, the mapping rule and an explicit output format, which is exactly what a panel needs.

options.text: Remove the job description from the prompt so Claude is not distracted by the technical requirements, and ask for general management questions.
options.why: The job description is the most valuable context in the prompt; removing it produces generic questions unrelated to this role.

options.text: Paste the job description again and add "Only ask about things in this document."
options.why: Restricting Claude to the document helps a little, but the prompt still says nothing about quantity, structure, question type or how the panel will use the output.

explanation: A strong business prompt combines a role, the source material, precise scope (how many, what kind, mapped to what) and the output format the downstream user needs. Restricting or repeating the source is not a substitute for saying what you actually want.
reference: Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct; Give Claude a role; Control the format of responses

stem: An operations analyst asks Claude to turn a pasted list of 40 vendors into a scorecard. The result scores some vendors out of 5 and others out of 10, and adds an "overall" column whose calculation is never explained. Which two additions to the prompt most directly fix these problems? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add "Be accurate and consistent" at the top of the prompt.
options.why: A general instruction to be consistent does not tell Claude which scale or which criteria to be consistent about.

options.text: Define the criteria (cost, reliability, lead time), the 1-to-5 scale for each, and how the overall score is calculated.
options.why: Explicit criteria and scales remove the ambiguity that caused mixed scales, and a stated formula stops Claude inventing an overall score.

options.text: Ask Claude to add a confidence rating next to every score.
options.why: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable quality signal and does nothing to make the scales consistent.

options.text: Include two example rows filled in exactly the way the finished scorecard should look.
options.why: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format and structure; Claude will mirror the columns, scale and style shown.

options.text: Paste the vendor list twice so Claude pays closer attention to it.
options.why: Duplicating input adds length without adding any instruction about scoring; the inconsistency came from missing rules, not from inattention.

options.text: Tell Claude it is the world's best procurement analyst.
options.why: A role can sharpen tone and focus, but a role alone does not define the criteria, the scale or the formula the scorecard needs.

explanation: When output is inconsistent, the usual cause is that the prompt left the rules implicit. Spell out the criteria, scale and calculations, and show an example of the finished format. Adjectives, confidence ratings, repetition and grand role titles do not supply the missing specification.
reference: Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct; Use examples effectively

stem: A consultant must turn a 60-page market report into a summary for a client's CFO. The summary must be no more than 300 words, must contain only figures that appear in the report, and must flag anything the report leaves unclear rather than guess. Which prompt satisfies all three requirements?

options.text: "Summarize the attached report for a CFO in no more than 300 words, focusing on financial implications. Use only figures that appear in the report and give the page for each. If the report does not answer something, say so instead of estimating."
options.why: It states audience, a hard length limit, a source restriction with page references that make checking easy, and an explicit "out" so Claude flags gaps instead of inventing figures.

options.text: "Summarize this report for a CFO. Be concise, be accurate, and double-check every number."
options.why: "Concise" and "accurate" are not measurable constraints; there is no word limit, no source restriction and no instruction for handling gaps.

options.text: "Summarize this report in 300 words for a CFO, and fill any gaps with typical industry benchmarks so the summary feels complete."
options.why: Filling gaps with outside benchmarks directly violates the rule that only figures from the report may appear.

options.text: "Summarize this report in 300 words for a CFO."
options.why: It covers audience and length but says nothing about sourcing figures or what to do when the report is unclear, so Claude may fill gaps from general knowledge.

explanation: Constraints must be stated explicitly and measurably: a word limit, a rule about which sources may be used, and an instruction that gives Claude permission to say "the report does not cover this". Giving Claude that out is a documented way to reduce fabricated details.
reference: Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct; Long context prompting (ground responses in quotes)

stem: A communications lead wrote a prompt that drafts the weekly all-hands announcement. It works well for her, so she shares the exact text with six colleagues, who paste it verbatim. Their outputs vary wildly: some are 800 words, some are jokey, and two mention confidential project names that should not appear. Which change makes the prompt reliable across all users?

options.text: Tell each colleague to add the line "match the tone and length of last week's announcement" before running the prompt.
options.why: Claude does not see last week's announcement unless it is in the chat, a Project or memory; the instruction points at context that is not there.

options.text: Add "Do not include confidential information" and "use good judgment about tone and length" to the prompt.
options.why: Claude cannot know which project names are confidential, and "good judgment" reintroduces the ambiguity that produced the variation.

options.text: Have everyone turn on extended thinking so Claude reasons more carefully about what the announcement should contain.
options.why: More reasoning cannot recover requirements that exist only in the author's head; the prompt itself is underspecified.

options.text: Rewrite the prompt to state the audience, a hard word limit, a short example paragraph showing the tone, labelled input fields each user must fill in, and a rule that only projects listed in those fields may be named.
options.why: The author's private context is made explicit: tone is shown by example, length is a number, and the confidentiality rule becomes checkable because allowed names are enumerated in the input.

explanation: A prompt that works for its author often relies on context the author supplies implicitly. To make it work for others, externalise that context: show tone with an example, replace judgment calls with measurable limits, and turn a rule Claude cannot verify ("nothing confidential") into one it can ("only names in the input").
reference: Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct (golden rule); Use examples effectively; Structure prompts with XML tags

stem: A project manager pastes three meeting transcripts into one message and asks Claude to extract action items, assign owners, build a risk register and draft the weekly status email, all at once. The response is a shallow mix that misses several actions. What is the best next approach?

options.text: Work in steps: extract and review the action items first, then build the risk register, then draft the email from the reviewed outputs.
options.why: Splitting a complex request into substeps lets each step get Claude's full attention and gives the manager a checkpoint before the next step builds on it.

options.text: Run the identical prompt in three separate chats, then merge the action items, risks and email from whichever outputs look most complete into one document.
options.why: Repeating an overloaded request produces three shallow answers to choose between; it does not fix the structure of the ask.

options.text: Resend the same message with "Be thorough and do not miss anything" added.
options.why: An exhortation does not change the fact that four different outputs are competing for attention in one response.

options.text: Combine the three transcripts into a single paragraph before pasting so Claude has less to read.
options.why: Removing structure from the input makes extraction harder, and the request is still asking for four deliverables at once.

explanation: The help centre advises breaking complex requests into substeps. Sequencing extract, then analyse, then draft produces better work at each stage and lets a human check intermediate outputs before they feed the next step.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer (break down complex requests into substeps)

stem: A curriculum designer wants Claude's help building a 12-week professional course: weekly lesson plans, an assessment for each week and a final rubric. Which decomposition is most likely to produce a coherent course?

options.text: Ask for all twelve weeks, their assessments and the final rubric in one prompt, with instructions to keep terminology, difficulty progression and formatting consistent across the whole course.
options.why: One enormous request spreads attention thin; consistency comes from a shared, approved outline, not from generating everything in a single response.

options.text: First produce the course outline and learning objectives and approve them; then generate lessons week by week against that outline; then write assessments aligned to the objectives.
options.why: An approved outline becomes the shared reference for every later step, so lessons and assessments are generated against fixed objectives rather than drifting.

options.text: Generate the assessments first, then ask Claude to write lessons that would let students pass them.
options.why: Assessments should be derived from learning objectives; starting with tests inverts the design and leaves the course without agreed goals.

options.text: Open a separate chat for each week and ask for that week's lesson with no reference to the other weeks.
options.why: Twelve unconnected chats have no shared objectives, so the weeks overlap, contradict each other or leave gaps.

explanation: Good decomposition orders the steps so each one produces an output the next depends on, and puts a human review at the points where a mistake would propagate. Outline and objectives first, then content, then assessment is the natural chain for course design.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer; Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct (sequential steps)

stem: An operations manager is using Claude to redesign an employee onboarding process in four stages: document the current process, identify bottlenecks, propose a new process, and draft the change announcement. Which two practices make this chained approach work well? (Choose two.)

options.text: Have each stage produce a clearly defined output, such as a numbered list of bottlenecks, that becomes the explicit input to the next stage.
options.why: Defined handoffs are what make a chain work; the next prompt can reference a concrete list rather than a vague earlier conversation.

options.text: Skip the documentation stage, since Claude can infer the current process from the bottleneck analysis.
options.why: Claude cannot know a company's actual process unless it is supplied; skipping the input stage means the analysis is built on guesses.

options.text: Review and correct each stage's output before feeding it into the next, because an error early in the chain propagates to everything after it.
options.why: Checkpoints between stages are the main benefit of decomposition; a missed bottleneck in stage two would otherwise silently shape the proposal and the announcement.

options.text: Run all four stages in separate chats without sharing outputs, so each stage is not biased by the previous one.
options.why: The stages depend on one another; isolating them removes the information each needs and produces a proposal unrelated to the identified bottlenecks.

options.text: Use the most capable model for the first stage and the fastest model for the rest, since later stages are just formatting.
options.why: Proposing a new process is the hardest reasoning step, not formatting; model choice is not what makes a chain succeed, defined handoffs and review are.

explanation: Chaining works when each step has a single clear goal, a defined output that the next step consumes, and a human check in between. Dropping inputs, isolating steps or treating later steps as trivial undermines the chain.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer; Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

stem: Two consultants are writing a 200-page RFP response over ten days. Every section must reflect the same three "win themes" and the same style guide, and the sections will be drafted at different times by different people. Which plan best meets these constraints?

options.text: Draft every section in one long chat that both consultants take turns using over the ten days, so Claude keeps all the context.
options.why: A ten-day chat grows until it degrades or hits the length limit, and two people sharing one thread lose track of which instructions are current.

options.text: Paste the entire RFP into a single prompt and ask Claude to write the complete response in one pass.
options.why: A 200-page deliverable in one response gives no checkpoints, and quality drops as the request grows; this is the opposite of decomposition.

options.text: Agree the win themes and style guide first, store them as Project instructions and knowledge, then draft each section in its own chat inside the Project and review it before moving on.
options.why: The shared foundation is created once and persists for both people, each section is a bounded task with its own review, and no chat needs to carry the whole history.

options.text: Have each consultant draft sections in plain chats, retyping the win themes from memory at the start of each session.
options.why: Retyping the themes from memory guarantees drift between sections and people; the shared context should be stored, not re-improvised.

explanation: Large collaborative deliverables need two things: a stable shared foundation (themes, style) that every step sees, and bounded steps with review. Storing the foundation in a Project and drafting sections in separate chats delivers both; one giant chat or one giant prompt delivers neither.
reference: Claude Help Center — What are Projects; My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer

stem: A marketing analyst built a five-step chain: (1) categorise 300 customer comments, (2) count comments per category, (3) pick the top three themes, (4) write insights, (5) draft an executive summary. The summary names "shipping delays" as the top theme. She checks step 2's table: Claude reported shipping 71 and pricing 40. When she tallies step 1's categorised list herself, pricing has 88 and shipping 52. What should she change?

options.text: Add "count carefully and double-check your totals" to the step 2 prompt and re-run the chain.
options.why: Asking a language model to count 300 items more carefully still relies on it tallying in prose; the failure mode is structural, not a lack of care.

options.text: Collapse steps 2 to 5 into one prompt so Claude sees the categorised list and the summary together.
options.why: Merging steps hides the intermediate table that made the error visible and still leaves the counting to the model.

options.text: Do the tally deterministically, in a spreadsheet or by having Claude compute it with its analysis tool from the categorised list, then re-run steps 3 to 5 from the corrected counts.
options.why: Counting is a deterministic step that should be done by a tool, not estimated in prose; once the counts are right, only the downstream steps need repeating.

options.text: Re-run step 2 on the most capable model with extended thinking turned on, since a stronger model reasoning more carefully will count the 300 comments more accurately than the current one.
options.why: A stronger model reduces but does not remove the risk of arithmetic drift over hundreds of items, and it leaves an unverifiable step in the chain.

explanation: Decomposition exposes which step failed, and the fix should match the step's nature. Language models are strong at categorising and writing but should not be trusted to tally hundreds of items in prose; move deterministic work to a tool, verify the intermediate output, and re-run only what depends on it.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer; Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

stem: A communications specialist asks Claude for a press release and gets a draft that is too long and reads like an advertisement. What is the best next step?

options.text: Send the identical prompt again, since Claude's outputs vary from run to run and a second attempt may land closer to the tone and length she has in mind.
options.why: Repeating the same prompt gives Claude no new information about what was wrong, so the next draft is likely to have the same problems.

options.text: Ask Claude "Is this good?" and send the draft if it says yes.
options.why: Claude's self-assessment is not a reliable quality check, and the specialist already knows what is wrong with the draft.

options.text: Start a new chat and paste the original prompt in again.
options.why: A new chat discards the draft and the context without changing the underspecified request.

options.text: Reply with specific feedback: cut to 250 words, remove superlatives, lead with the customer impact, and keep the CEO quote.
options.why: Concrete follow-up instructions tell Claude exactly what to change and what to preserve, which is how the help centre recommends refining an answer.

explanation: Iteration means giving Claude feedback it can act on: what to cut, what to add, what to keep. Retrying the same prompt, restarting, or asking Claude to grade itself does not communicate what was wrong.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer (give Claude feedback)

stem: An HR coordinator asks Claude to draft an FAQ about the company's new parental-leave policy. Several answers are wrong, for example the number of paid weeks. She realises she never gave Claude the policy. Which iteration fixes the root cause?

options.text: Paste the policy document, ask Claude to answer every question only from it, and to list any question the document does not answer.
options.why: The output was wrong because context was missing; supplying the source, restricting answers to it and asking for gaps to be flagged addresses exactly that.

options.text: Reply "Some of these are wrong, please try again and be more accurate."
options.why: Claude still has no source for the policy; asking for accuracy without supplying the facts invites a different set of guesses.

options.text: Rephrase the request as "Write an FAQ for our generous new parental-leave policy, written by an experienced HR professional" so Claude has a clearer picture of the role and tone.
options.why: Rewording the request with an adjective adds no facts; the number of paid weeks is still unknown to Claude.

options.text: Ask Claude to mark each answer with a confidence score so she can fix only the low-confidence ones.
options.why: Confidence scores do not make answers correct, and a confident wrong answer about leave entitlement is the most dangerous kind.

explanation: When an output is factually wrong, ask why: usually Claude lacked the source. The right iteration supplies the missing context, constrains Claude to it, and asks it to say what the source does not cover, rather than pleading for accuracy.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer (provide context); Prompting best practices — Long context prompting

stem: A project manager uses Claude every Friday to draft a status report for the steering committee. The first few drafts needed heavy editing. Which two iteration techniques will most effectively improve the drafts over the coming weeks? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ask Claude to critique its own draft against a short checklist (audience, missing risks, jargon) and then revise it before she reads it.
options.why: A structured self-review against explicit criteria catches predictable problems in a second pass and is a recognised way to improve a first draft.

options.text: Regenerate the draft five times each week and pick the one that feels best.
options.why: Repeated generation without feedback is a lottery; it does not teach the prompt anything and wastes usage.

options.text: Collect the edits the committee sponsor makes each week and turn them into explicit rules in the prompt, such as "always open with the RAG status and one-line reason".
options.why: Converting observed corrections into instructions is the core loop of iteration: each round tightens the prompt so the next draft needs less editing.

options.text: Tell Claude "the previous drafts were bad" without saying why, so it tries a different style.
options.why: Feedback without specifics gives Claude nothing to change deliberately; it will guess at a new style that may be worse.

options.text: Ask Claude to rate its confidence in the draft from 1 to 10 and only edit drafts that score below 7.
options.why: Self-reported confidence is not a reliable measure of quality and would let poor drafts through unedited.

options.text: Switch to a different model each week to see which one guesses the committee's preferences best.
options.why: The committee's preferences are unknown to every model until they are written into the prompt; model roulette is not iteration.

explanation: Effective iteration is a feedback loop: have Claude check its work against explicit criteria, and convert every human correction into a rule the prompt states next time. Regeneration, vague complaints, confidence scores and model-hopping do not close the loop.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer (give Claude feedback); Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

stem: A consulting team's SWOT-analysis prompt produces a good result about four times in five, but occasionally it ignores the rule that every point must cite the section of the client document it came from. The team needs it reliable for six analysts and has time for only one or two more iterations. Which change is most likely to fix it?

options.text: Change the instruction to "You MUST ALWAYS cite the section for every point; this is mandatory and non-negotiable" in capital letters, and repeat it at the top and bottom of the prompt so it cannot be missed.
options.why: Emphasis alone is a weak, probabilistic fix; it does not show Claude what a correct entry looks like or add a check before the answer is returned.

options.text: Move the citation rule next to the output format, add one example entry showing the citation style, and ask Claude to check every entry has a citation before it finishes.
options.why: Putting the rule with the format, showing it by example and adding a self-check turns an easily skipped instruction into a structural part of the output.

options.text: Have each analyst generate five SWOTs and keep the one where the citations are present.
options.why: Manual selection among repeated runs multiplies effort and usage for six people and does nothing to improve the prompt.

options.text: Switch the team to the most capable model so the rule is followed more often.
options.why: A stronger model may help at the margin, but the instruction is still buried and unexemplified; the reliable fix is in the prompt, not the tier.

explanation: When an instruction is followed intermittently, restructure rather than shout: place the rule where it applies, demonstrate it with an example, and ask Claude to verify its output against the rule. These changes make compliance part of the format instead of a hope.
reference: Prompting best practices — Use examples effectively; Control the format of responses

stem: A marketing manager has revised a customer-segment description six times in one chat, changing her mind about tone, length and which segments to include along the way. Each new version is further from what she wants, and the latest one reintroduces a segment she removed three messages ago. What is happening, and what should she do?

options.text: The model is too fast to keep up; switch to a slower, more capable model in the same chat and ask for one more revision.
options.why: The problem is contradictory instructions accumulated in the conversation, which a different model would inherit unchanged.

options.text: Reply "ignore everything I said before" and restate the requirements in the same chat.
options.why: Earlier turns remain in the context and still influence the response; a verbal instruction to ignore them is unreliable.

options.text: The chat now contains conflicting instructions that pull the output in different directions; start a fresh chat with one consolidated prompt stating the current requirements and an example of the desired result.
options.why: Consolidating the surviving requirements into a clean prompt removes the contradictory history that is causing the drift, and the example anchors the target.

options.text: Ask Claude to list what it thinks she wants, confirm it, and continue revising in the same chat.
options.why: Confirming the requirements is useful, but the conflicting turns stay in context and the abandoned segment can resurface again.

explanation: Iterating in one long chat can backfire once instructions contradict each other: everything said earlier is still in context. When drift sets in, consolidate what you actually want into a single prompt with an example and start a fresh chat, rather than adding a seventh correction on top.
reference: Claude Help Center — How do usage and length limits work; Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

stem: An events coordinator wants ideas for the theme of next year's customer conference. Which prompt approach is best suited to this brainstorming task?

options.text: Ask Claude for the single best theme with a full justification.
options.why: Asking for one answer up front narrows the search before any options have been seen; brainstorming needs breadth first.

options.text: Ask for 20 varied theme ideas with a one-line description each and no evaluation, then filter them in a second prompt using agreed criteria.
options.why: Brainstorming works best as quantity and variety first, then a separate pass that judges the ideas against criteria.

options.text: Ask Claude to cite a dated source for every theme idea.
options.why: Sources and dates matter for research tasks; ideas for a conference theme are not factual claims that need citations.

options.text: Ask Claude to present three carefully selected theme ideas as a formal memo addressed to the leadership team, each with a budget estimate and a risk assessment.
options.why: A polished memo format belongs to a drafting task; at the idea stage it adds ceremony and slows the exploration down.

explanation: Different task types call for different prompting strategies. Brainstorming rewards asking for many diverse options without judgment and filtering afterwards; research needs sources and dates; drafting needs audience and tone; analysis needs data and criteria.
reference: Claude Help Center — My prompt isn't giving me a helpful answer; Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct

stem: A communications lead needs to know how three competitors currently describe their sustainability commitments on their websites, for a board briefing next week. Which prompting approach fits this research task?

options.text: Use web search or Research, ask for each competitor's current wording with the source URL and retrieval date, and have Claude separate what the sources state from its own inferences.
options.why: Research tasks need current, sourced facts; asking for URLs, dates and a fact-versus-inference split makes the output checkable before it reaches the board.

options.text: Ask Claude to brainstorm 20 sustainability commitments the competitors might plausibly have made.
options.why: Plausible inventions are the opposite of what a board briefing needs; this is a research question, not an ideation exercise.

options.text: Ask Claude to draft the board briefing straight away, including whatever it knows about the competitors.
options.why: Drafting before researching bakes unverified and possibly outdated claims into the deliverable.

options.text: Ask Claude from its training knowledge with no dates, since the sustainability pages of large companies rarely change and searching would slow the answer down and add unnecessary usage.
options.why: Training knowledge may be stale and unsourced; for competitor statements that change often, the answer must come from live sources.

explanation: For research tasks the prompt should demand sources, retrieval dates and a clear line between what the source says and what Claude infers, and should use web search or Research so the facts are current. Drafting or brainstorming prompts are the wrong tool for a factual question.
reference: Claude Help Center — Use research on Claude; When should I use web search, extended thinking, and research?

stem: An operations lead uploads a quarterly incident log (about 400 rows) and wants Claude to analyse it. Which two elements matter most in a prompt for an analysis task like this? (Choose two.)

options.text: State the specific questions and criteria, such as "rank causes by frequency and by total downtime, and flag any cause that grew quarter over quarter".
options.why: Analysis prompts need explicit questions and criteria; without them Claude decides what is interesting and the output may not answer what the business needs.

options.text: Ask Claude to write the findings in a persuasive, upbeat tone.
options.why: Tone instructions belong to drafting tasks; for analysis, a persuasive framing can distort what the data shows.

options.text: Ask Claude to show how it derived each figure and to state any assumptions it made about the data.
options.why: Showing the working makes the analysis verifiable and surfaces assumptions, such as how missing values were treated, before the numbers are relied on.

options.text: Ask for 30 alternative explanations of the incidents without evaluating any of them.
options.why: Unfiltered idea generation is a brainstorming pattern; an analysis task needs conclusions grounded in the data.

options.text: Tell Claude to estimate values for any rows with missing fields so the analysis is complete.
options.why: Inventing data to fill gaps corrupts the analysis; missing data should be reported, not fabricated.

explanation: Analysis prompts should supply the data, spell out the questions and criteria, and require transparent working and stated assumptions. Tone, unfiltered ideation and gap-filling belong to other task types or are harmful here.
reference: Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct; Long context prompting

stem: A school administrator reuses the prompt she normally uses for data analysis ("analyse this thoroughly and cover every angle") to write a letter to parents about a timetable change. She gets 900 words of analysis with no letter. The letter must be under 200 words, warm and plain, and end with what parents need to do. Which prompt fits the task?

options.text: "Research how other schools have communicated timetable changes, with sources, and summarise the best practices."
options.why: This is a research prompt; it produces a sourced summary of practices, not the letter she needs to send.

options.text: "List 15 different ways we could explain the timetable change to parents."
options.why: Brainstorming options is useful earlier in a process, but the task now is to produce one finished letter.

options.text: "Analyse the timetable change and explain all its implications for pupils, staff and families thoroughly and from every angle, then write something suitable for parents based on the analysis at the end."
options.why: It repeats the analysis framing that caused the problem and still specifies no audience details, tone, length or call to action.

options.text: "Write a letter to parents, under 200 words, warm and plain, explaining the change on 1 March and ending with the two things they need to do. Match the tone of the pasted letter from last term."
options.why: A drafting prompt names the audience, tone, length, key facts and call to action, and supplies a tone example, which is exactly what drafting tasks need.

explanation: Drafting tasks need audience, tone, length, the key facts and the desired action, ideally with an example of the voice to match. Reusing an analysis-style prompt produces analysis; the strategy must change with the task type.
reference: Prompting best practices — Be clear and direct; Use examples effectively

stem: A consultant asks Claude in one prompt: "Find out what our three main competitors changed in their pricing this year, propose five ways we could respond, and write a one-page recommendation for the executive team." The result has no sources, only two response options, and reads like a blog post. The deliverable must be sourced, must consider a genuinely broad set of responses, and must be in executive tone. Which approach satisfies all three?

options.text: Keep the single prompt but add "cite your sources, be creative, and write like an executive".
options.why: Bolting three adjectives onto one prompt still asks Claude to research, ideate and draft in one breath; the three task types need different structures, not more adjectives.

options.text: Ask for the one-page recommendation first, then ask Claude to add sources for the claims it made.
options.why: Adding citations after the fact invites Claude to find or invent sources that fit conclusions already written, the reverse of evidence-led work.

options.text: Brainstorm the five responses first, then use Research to find pricing changes that justify them, then draft.
options.why: Ideating before researching means the options are not grounded in what competitors actually did, and the research becomes a search for confirmation.

options.text: Run three prompts in sequence: a Research prompt for the pricing changes with sources and dates; a brainstorming prompt for at least ten responses, then filter to five against stated criteria; and a drafting prompt with audience, length and tone that uses only the verified findings.
options.why: Each stage uses the prompting strategy its task type needs, research feeds ideation and ideation feeds drafting, so the final page is sourced, broad and appropriately written.

explanation: A request that mixes research, brainstorming and drafting should be split so each part gets the right strategy: sources and dates for research, quantity-then-filter for ideation, audience and tone for drafting. Order matters too: evidence first, then options, then the write-up.
